title: Most Wins After Reordering
statement:
You get an array nums. Make a copy, then rearrange the copy in any order you like and call it perm. Position i is a win if perm[i] > nums[i], strictly.

Return the largest number of wins any rearrangement can achieve. The original nums stays in its order.

examples.why: For example perm = [3, 1, 5, 2, 3]: 3 > 2, 5 > 3 and 3 > 1 win. Nothing can beat the 5, and the two 3s cannot both be beaten as well, since only one value (5) exceeds 3.
Every value is equal, and a tie is not a win.
The two 2s can beat the two 1s; nothing can beat a 2.

hints: Sort a copy. The order of nums does not matter for the count, only which values you pair with which.
To beat a small value, use the smallest value that still beats it. Wasting a big value on a small target can cost you a later win.
Sort, then use two pointers: one over the targets (smallest first) and one over the candidates. Whenever the candidate beats the current target, count a win and move to the next target.

explain.intuition:
Positions do not matter, only the pairing does: each value of perm is matched against one value of nums. So sort the values. Now think like a card game where you want to beat as many of your opponent's cards as possible: beat their weakest cards first, each with your cheapest card that still wins. Any win you get with a stronger card could also be had with the cheaper one, keeping the strong card free.

With both lists the same sorted array, one pointer i marks the weakest target not yet beaten. Walk through the values as candidates; whenever a candidate is strictly bigger than sorted[i], that is a win and i moves on. A neat consequence: the answer equals n minus the count of the most frequent value.
steps: For each value x in sorted order, if x > sorted[i], increment i.
Return i, the number of targets beaten.
pitfalls: Pairing each value with the next distinct value only once, so duplicates are undercounted. In [1, 1, 2, 2] both 2s win.
Trying to keep the original positions while matching. Reordering means only the multiset of values matters.

solutions.title: Try every rearrangement
solutions.idea: Generate every permutation and count its wins. Only for tiny inputs.

solutions.title: Sort and greedily beat the weakest
solutions.idea: Sorted ascending, each value beats the weakest target it can; a pointer tracks the next target.

solutions.title: n minus the biggest frequency
solutions.idea: Only copies of the most common value are forced to lose; every other target can be beaten.

followups: Prove that the answer is n minus the largest frequency.
You must beat a different array than your own: given rival and yours, maximize wins. Does the same greedy work?
